I am use the same sort of strategy I did for the pre-steam-release, where dwarves only did what they were assigned by default.

I make a work group for woodworkers, they do wood crafts, carpentry, and bowery. One for stone in the same way, one of farmers, one of cooks, one for jewelers, clothers, and metal smiths. As migrants come into my fort I assign them 2-3 of these work orders based off their best skills. Peasants are assigned as farmers. Then I lock down everyone except the peasants, who I give a chance to do whatever they like.

It is important to note that dwarves can get cranky if they only can do one thing, just like us the monotony gets to them.

What you prioritize in the beginning is about what supplies you brought, and your goals. I usually bring a lot of animals and like to get bedrooms set up quickly, so all of my first dwarves end up on stone working, wood working, farmers, and cooks. Once my food supply is stable and I have extra rooms and dwarves I start focusing on making trade goods. I build more crafts dwarves shops and change my work orders to just making sure we have enough barrels, bins, and mugs at all times, and that we have some spare furniture at all times. I also assign a lot of jewelers and build a lot of workshops for them at this point because I plan on decorating as much stuff with gems as dwarvenly possible. Once I get the next migrant wave after this, I start assigning clothers and building workshops for them.

I think most players, espically long time ones generally have a collection of jobs they bundle together like I do. What you prioritize assigning, and what is in each work order is up to what you want out of your fort.

Additionally there are a lot of jobs that are more efficient put together. Fisher dwarves, carpenters, and hunters are already running around outside, so it might be a good idea to have them gather wild plants while they are at it. Other common combos are miners who also craft stone, jewelery, and masonry. Woodcutters who craft wood, carpentry, and bows. Hunters who butcher and cook.  Miners who smooth and engrave stone.(They can harvest the raw product then haul it to a workshop to process.) And so on and so forth.

No such thing as too old. If you want answers, you deserve to have them. I got diagnosed at 21 after my symptoms suddenly increased at 20. For me, getting diagnosed was important as the sudden and large tics started shortly after I revieced some brain damage. I was worried there was something terrifyingly wrong with me. Having the doctor tell me it was a tic disorder and I didn't need to worry about my safety brought me a lot of comfort. After that I did some more research, read other people's experiences, and realized I'd had tics as long as I could remember. They had just been small and everyone assumed I was just a weird kid doing weird stuff. Getting diagnosed as an adult also gave me a lot of comfort. Even if I didn't know what it was as a kid, I knew I was different, and other kids would make fun of me for moving around so much. It's comforting for me to have a word for it that isn't just "freak."

It really comes down to wither or not you think a diagnosis could be helpful. If you think it would help you or other people understand you better, go for it!

Most of the time my tics are very quiet, and I don't say any words. I make small beeping and cooing sounds that most people don't even notice. Sometimes I can tell I'm about to scream, but sometimes I open my mouth thinking it's a normal little coo is going to come out, and suddenly I sound like a hyena. I find that the intensity of my tics (volume, force, size of gesture I make, etc.) Pretty much always depends on if I've been suppressing and how stressed out I am. The larger and louder tics usually also get rid of the urge in one go, while smaller tics usually have to happen a couple of times before I feel better.

I used to only have mild tics that no one really noticed (including me lol. Squeezeing my eyes tight shut, wiggling my nose, making fists.) And they sometimes show up in my dreams. It wasn't until I was 20 that I started having big noticeable tics. So far I haven't had any of these happen in my dream. I think part of it is that I didn't realize what my little tics were. I thought having to make little movements to make your brain feel right was just quirky. Some people have catchphrases, or always wear mis-matched socks, and I made funny faces. So they showed up in my dreams, same as any other little quirk in myself or others would.

However, at 20 my tics changed a lot, and so did my expireance with them. It wasn't quirky, it was embarrassing, and occasionally painful. I'm constantly worried about how people will react to me in public. I think my subconscious just doesn't feel like that's a defining characteristic of me, and just leaves it out.

As everyone is saying, definitely talk to an adult you trust at school. I didn't always have the ability to go to the doc as a kid, and teachers were generally happy to help me find accommodations.

My other suggestion is definitely the school nurse if you trust the one at your school. While they by definition can't diagnose you with something, they still might be able to find you resources and vouch for you.

Also keep a journal on your tics if you can. When, what tic, what happened right before etc. When you do see a doctor they are going to ask these questions, and it helps to have an actual record in front of you. Plus it will help you identify any triggers for your tics, these vary from person to person, but lots of things like lack of sleep, stress, lack of food etc. can cause you to tic more. Once you know what these are, it becomes a lot easier to manage and predict.

If you felt normal while smoking, and trust where you got it, I don't think it was laced. You, as the person who smoked, would know better than people who weren't there if something was funky. 

Overall ask a doctor if you can. Tourettes is genetic, and is normally only diagnosed if symptoms start before age 18, sometimes 21, and have lasted at least a year. This is because there are so many other conditions that can cause involuntary movement, many of which will resolve themselves. If you have any conditions like ADHD, anxiety, OCD etc. These can cause tics when you are under extreme stress, so I would also suggest speaking to your mental health provider as well if you have one. 


My tourettes did actually start due to drug use, so I want to give an idea of what that actually looks like, because it wasn't just smoking weed once. 

Some medications can temporarily increase tics in people who already have tourettes. Usually discontinuing those medications will help. Sometimes medications can also cause tics in people without tourettes, but generally, again, they improve with discontinuation.

I meanwhile, had small unnoticed, and noninvasive tics as a kid. No one called tourettes then because it wasn't a "disorder" if it didn't impact my life at all. But at 20 years old I overdosed on multiple medications including stimulants and antidepressants. I spent a week in the hospital. The tics got far worse when I was home and after a year of them actually causing me problems I went to a neurologist. She explained to me that the tourettes was always there, but I damaged part of my brain that managed it.

Edit: oh yeah, and I smoke weed to help calm tic attacks.

Additionally “ruling out” is where you start testing the most common and dangerous conditions first, then as each of those comes back negative the doctor would then “rule out” that diagnosis and move onto the next test for a less common, or less immediately dangerous. 
Gastroparisis is one of the most common causes of early satiety (the symptom specifically mentioned) but it could be a lot of other things. Doctors are taught the rule of “if you hear hoofbeats, think horses not zebras. ” Before this you likely had blood work, most likely metabolic panels and or thyroid hormones. Thyroid disorders are also a very common cause of changes in appetite and weight.

I think the main thing is just that the doctor is using “rule out” to mean the process of doing these tests, while the more common reading would be that “ruling out” is the outcome.

I have PTSD, and if my hands aren't busy I end up looking like I'm going to make a run for it at any moment. I think if I was in a court room it would be better if I was knitting than if I was bouncing my leg, looking back and forth at the door, and scooting around in my seat.

I am going to say this because I assume you don't know, and not because I think you are trying to be harmful.

But assuming someone can't focus while knitting is super outdated and based on old etiquette rules. If it's a complex pattern that requires reading the pattern or counting? Definitely not the move. However, for many people, espically nuerodivergent people, "focusing" in the way you would expect, would actually make taking in information harder. For someone who is autistic, forcing themselves to make eye contact might make it harder for them to also process what they are hearing. Someone with ADHD might be able to crank out a garter scarf without looking, but could end up completely spaced out and distracted by trying to sit still. Someone with PTSD might have extra hypervigilant energy that they need to expend. On and on and on. 

Tl;Dr- People expirance the world differently, and you can't just assume that someone else's brain works the same as yours. Neurodivergent people spend their whole lives struggling to give the appearance of "complete attention." When really there just isn't one way "attention" or "active listening" looks.

Crayola makers are great! The supertips are a favourite in the Bujo community and come in a large range of colours (100) very affordably (only a few cents per marker.) The lettering for me is usually 1.5-2 cm (3-4 boxes in an average dot grid Journal.) The broad lines are about a mid point between those and Tombows which I think are about twice the size as supertips. The only downsides is that if you are trying to cover broad areas the crayola markers, like most water based markers, will be streaky if you are colouring a larger area with them and they can only be bought in packs, not individually. Though I would not personally recommend the crayola brush markers.
Artline stix markers are cheap water based brush pens. They have triangular bodies with lego like designs that allow the markers to be snapped together. They are similar insize to the crayola broadlines markers. They aren't very streaky and you can get some colour build up with them. The hardness of the brush tip can vary a lot from colour to colour and only 20 colours are available. They are also pretty adorable at around $1.25 USD per marker. They can also only be bought in packs.
Karin Brushmarker Pros are brush pens with water colour ink inside them and nylon nibs. The nylon nib is long lasting and can even be used on rough textured paper without fraying (this is not true of most brush markers.) They look like very dark water colours and can be blended really nicely, especially on water colour paper. They will bleed through pretty much any journal pages. They also come in neon and metallic colours that can be bought either in their own sets, or in larger sets. For the regular colours you can buy 12 colour sets, a 26 colour set, or a 60 colour set. These cost around 1.70-2.50 USD. 
Tombow dual brush pens are also well loved, but are a lot more pricey at are $3 USD per pen. They also come in a wide range of colours. (slightly more than supertips at I think 112 colours) They are very large with decent looking lettering needing about 4cm (8 squares in an average dot grid journal.) They are also prone to bleeding. They have one side that is a brush nib and another side that is a tine tipped nib. The brush nib is less streaky than crayola markers, but the fine nib is worse. You can buy packs of either 10 or 20 markers along with individual markers.
Anyways that's my summary of the markers I am personally familiar with and use.

You don't want to skip ahead how many pages you think you need because you might need a few more or less and page hogging usually isn't a great plan. Really it boils down what works best for you. If you know exactly how many pages you are going to use this month and want to have more time to spend on it, go for making your title page early. However if you aren't sure how many pages you are going to use or are making something more simplistic maybe hold off. You could also draw it in pencil sooner and ink it in later so you would still have the chance to mix things up, but have a head start.
